title: Influence of surgery and critical illness on the microbial community
summary: The purpose of this study is to examine how heart surgery affects the bacterial composition in the gut, also known as the microbiome. Such surgery can cause a strong inflammatory reaction in the body, which may harm the gut microbiome and its interaction with the rest of the body. We want to find out how the diversity of bacteria in the gut changes after heart surgery, with and without the use of a heart-lung machine, and what effects these changes may have on the immune system. We are also interested in whether these changes influence how long patients stay in the hospital, the amount of certain bacterial substances in the blood, the level of inflammation in the body, and how well the immune system works. To do this, each study participant will provide a stool sample and a blood sample before and after surgery. These samples will be examined in specialized laboratories. The results will then be compared with samples from a group of healthy volunteers who also provided stool and blood samples.
conditions: Severe Inflammatory Response Syndrome, intestinal bacterial overgrowth

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
- cardiac surgery with median sternotomy
Exclusion criteria:
- positive pregnancy test
- heart failure (NYHA class III or higher)
- peripheral arterial disease stage IIb or higher
- chronic respiratory insufficiency requiring oxygen therapy
- pharmacological immunosuppression
- current treatment for malignancy
- history of major intestinal surgery
- chronic inflammatory bowel disease
- dependency on / affiliation with the study team
- vomiting and/or diarrhea within the past month (three or more episodes)
